title: Nuclear War: A Scenario
author: Annie Jacobsen
review:
DNF. 

Two years ago I went to an Islam & AI conference where the main speaker that everyone went to see, a shaykh, turned everything into a conversation about nuclear war. He kept recommending this book warning us to prepare for the inevitable.

A few years into the genocide of Palestinians I couldn’t read this - we got to see in a few chapters how prepared the U.S. is if nuclear war would happen - something that may not have existed in the first place if we didn’t invent these weapons. The US because it manufactures all these weapons has the ability to work on preventing them through all sorts of policies & institutions. Likely, if we were to be struck by a nuke we wouldn’t follow policy like this because lol when are there gonna be actual drills on this. Why dont other countries get to build these institutions? How many countries need these policies to protect them from the U.S.? 

I kept thinking about the time I walked through a Hiroshima where I saw where the blast occurred, I witnessed the lone building they kept to show the destructive nature of nukes, and the burning candle in hopes that nukes never exist. Why did we do that? Why do we actively murder people abroad with WMDs and then tell others they can’t stockpile to defend themselves from… us? I keep thinking of all the nonstop images coming from Palestine and I’m like who gives a sh** if the U.S. has all these policies in place. I don’t need to imagine this scenario, because we unfortunately get to see what our tax dollars do every day to others abroad.

The book just made me think of the concept of “d**k measuring” contests that men do, all of this is so stupid.  It’s really hard to care about this when we’re constantly bombing People abroad. This book is ridiculous imagination of what would happen if we were attacked by nukes. It’s absurd, I don’t know why the shaykh recommended it, I feel like I have lost interest in this shaykh now. 

There’s this influencer on TikTok her name is @emma_pike_ who speaks on her area of expertise - nuclear disarmament - and she’s so much more interesting than this bizarre fearmongering book with no real purpose besides imagining the U.S., the inventor of the most destructive weapons ever created, is the victim.

“ Two strong minded women in a man’s world if they do not quickly become allies are destined to be incurable rivals.”

Not an important quote in the book, but one that made me think a lot about the author and how this book came to be. The back cover says the author was a corporate strategist, and the Machiavellian nature of the book shows it. You can imagine if there was no physical violence and magic, you’d be reading a book similar to the shows Industry or Succession. Everything reminds me of how it was like working with folks from McKinsey and BCG - always looking to understand motives, cynically selfish in one’s approach to others, and seeing those who don’t play the game as weak. 

The quote above really got to me as it’s true about working in a profession where it’s mostly men - you have to decide what the women are around you - and if at least one of you decides you’re a rival you’ll forever be a rival. 

I admit against my will that I enjoyed reading this, even though it’s not really the world I want to operate in.

title: Bad Therapy: Why the Kids Aren't Growing Up
author: Abigail Shrier
review:
The main takeaways from this book are - resilience is the norm not trauma from difficult experiences, the “professionalization” of relationships is resulting in us incapable of having good ones, and we need to stop talking about feelings — which result in us seeing ourselves as isolated entities, and instead remind ourselves that we exist in society. I saw this as “we” because although the book is about why children are not able to grow up, her lessons are easily applied to all of us in the West. 

For years, I have been questioning the negative externalities of a world that normalizes therapy as something everyone should do, and have been actively seeking authors who can really show evidence of it. The mental healthcare industry has enormous power over us as individuals and as we conceive of how society functions. Our over reliance on therapists results in us not feeling capable of navigating personal relationships without an “expert” to tell us what to do, and then we rely on the “expert” to handle our most private concerns which robs us of intimacy with close relationships. She goes into this. She also goes into the fact that many of us now when we see someone suffering we immediately offer advice that they see a therapist, without the real recognition that healing often comes through community - what does offloading of that burden do to all of us, especially children who are learning how to socialize? For children this means that they don’t effectively bond with each other, and instead become increasingly dependent on the adults around them. 

I was quite reflective on the idea that resilience is the norm, not trauma when it comes to responding to difficult situations - it made me think of my own journey in mental health where once I saw myself as resilient, not someone defined by my issues, I saw change. Are we infantilizing children by protecting them in every possible way from harm? I don’t know because I can’t really say that her generation ended up being raised better than the current generation, otherwise we wouldn’t have an author so dismissive of world events as something children shouldn’t care about. 

I also personally related to her thesis on how therapists can actively harm you (without intention) because we rely too much on their expertise - I had a therapist last year who told me session after session, in an effort to get rid of my anxiety, to not believe anything my mind is telling me unless I got concrete evidence. It caused me to spiral out of control for I lost my trust in my intuition, something that is a strength of mine. 

Even before that situation I’ve thought a lot about how over prescribed therapy is in every day situations - where we couch language in trauma and wellness and constantly remind people to not commit suicide can have an adverse effect - one in which she compares to the famous DARE programs which resulted in people increasing the amount of drugs they took because it aroused curiosity. One of the things I’d like to research on is whether those hotlines are effective in a good way, for I called the hotline and found myself talking to an individual who was clearly just going through a checklist of questions. Once I started feeling better I felt uncomfortable with the idea that if I see someone going through I crisis I should tell them to call a hotline. Who is measuring the effectiveness of these things we’re told are supposed to be helping? And why is everyone just getting more anxious and depressed when mental health therapy is such a norm to seek? Has the constant language around mental health made us more sick, because now we’re constantly evaluating our experiences in terms of whether it’s making us “happier?” And is the focus on happiness the wrong criteria because none of us are gleeful for even 20% of our days. 

We are consistently defining ourselves through our negative mental health, defining others through their mental health, which is actively harming our ability to be in community or even a healthy 1:1 relationship. By constantly talking about our personal feelings we’re becoming people who think our feelings need to be prioritized before existing amongst each other. The healthier option is to think less of ourselves, a lot of what she spoke of made me think of theology and how religion asks us to orient ourselves.

I was listening to her audio book and caught 9/10 of the signs of bad therapy and wanted to share them in the review:

1. Focus on what you’re feeling - being state oriented is detrimental over task orientation 
2. Rumination - habitually give voice to personal problems, obsessive over what went wrong 
3. Making happiness a goal, but reward emotional suffering - the more vigorously you approach happiness the lower your happiness. Identifying w your strengths is now socially seen as problematic bc it will demonstrate your privilege, whereas identifying with your struggles - the norm in high schools now - is problematic because people aren’t resolving them
4. Affirm kids worries - people are not using exposure therapy to help people, instead they create accommodation to their challenges 
5. Monitor, monitor, monitor - parents can never look away - need more intel. Kids are always under observation now - they have almost no privacy. Adding constant monitoring is adding stress to someone’s life. It’s creating anxiety 
6. Dispense diagnoses liberally - a diagnosis is something that says the person is sick. Creates a negative sense of self. 
7. Encourage kids to share trauma 
8. Encourage kids to cut off family - she has shown that increasingly there is encouragement to cut off relations 
9. Create treatment dependency - teaching people we are not adequate humans we need authority to tell us what to do 

Shrier also has a large focus on how we keep blaming parents for everything as if everything that is our problem is something as a result of our childhood issues. She eviscerates Bessel Van der Kolk and Gabor Mate for their push on how we’re all traumatized and how that negatively impacts our ability to be resilient. She argues that they effectively damaged the world by their push for seeing everything through the lens of trauma. We are so much more complex than what happened to us & blaming our parents for being idiots or bad parents isn’t the best solution. I am looking forward to this part of her thesis becoming mainstream as I believe our society has become a bit too focused on pattern recognition of our behaviors rather than actively having us reach towards healthier ways of being. (Note: she makes a disclaimer at the beginning of her book that this isn’t meant for people who do have serious mental health issues and are in need of medication or regular therapy)

Another point I appreciated she made was that scientists do not know that much about the brain. I remember reading Dr Thomas Insel’s book during an age where mental health startups were all the rage, where he  argues we need more metrics! We need more medication! But then couches that in a lot of we don’t know if this stuff is helping. I myself studied anti-depressants in grad school and was shocked at how little scientists knew of the effectiveness of them & yet they area consistently prescribed to the point that people are on them for decades. I kept thinking of scientism, the modern day worship of science (Dr Seyyed Hossein Nasr is a good start for this topic), where if a study comes out we believe it without scrutiny - which she argues has caused a lot of problems in our society - we need to scrutinize all of these studies more. She shares how significant psychological studies that we know about, such as the Bessel van der Kolk ones, fail basic scrutiny with biases embedded in the construction of the study, effectively making the study worthless. Many of these popular psychology theories are rooted in studies that we should question whether they really solved what they claim to have.

I think she doesn’t do enough to question why western society ended up where it is in terms of focusing on ourselves in an unhealthy matter. I kept thinking about the advent of abstract expressionism which changed western art forever, which was a response to the shock of nuclear war in ww2 - a dramatic movement towards individual feelings over the centuries of cultural symbolism. I left the book more fascinated by Islamic psychology and how it likely is a better solution to therapy than what the west comes up with - Dr Francesca Boca-Aldarque has some really great critiques on the western mental healthcare industry and how it’s harming us over on youtube. George Makari’s Soul Machine is an excellent book on how the west screwed up mental health through analyzing the history of separating the mind from the body, and the effect of that on our conception of the self. If we stop treating each other as you have X, and instead focus on how do we bring you back in balance, the language around how we conceive of ourselves likely could be healthier. 

That being said there were quite a few things I couldn’t get past - she’s clearly a conservative & her politics were very well enmeshed in her writing. She seems to ignore the realities of life that may result in mental health issues - lack of social mobility, less food, less jobs, less ability to imagine a future with climate change. She does address it by claiming that hardship makes us more resilient people, and I do understand her argument I just don’t know if I fully buy it. What if we are living on a doomed planet? What if mama really can’t afford to feed you today - I grew up in poverty but a loved one grew up in extreme poverty - where there were times she’d go outside to look for food - I don’t think that’s an experience of hardship that we can just claim is something that makes us stronger. There’s also scientific evidence that inflammation - and the diseases that come out of it - are a result of chronic stress. We know that chronic stress can cause chronic conditions, to assume it doesn’t debilitate our mental health and our lives makes no sense. 

There’s more a need to be within certain forms of behavior - with the rise of AI behavioral control is more important. We are under surveillance more often so we don’t have the ability to make even small mistakes. She kept quoting Israeli psychologists and the Israeli way of living and I kept wondering how seriously can we take how they’re raising their kids when their children are actively committing genocide? She reminded me a bit of George Lakoff’s book Don’t Think of the Elephant where he discusses the differences between conservative and liberal ways of wanting to raise children - she’s clearly in the camp that is patriarchal authoritative. She made some ridiculous claim that the amount of authoritarian parents has diminished and those studies are irrelevant now, I literally witnessed a child being smacked in the head with a shoe by their parent, I have no idea where she claims that this world doesn’t exist in America anymore. Stats on abuse have not decreased so how can we imagine that the authoritarian way of parenting has been eliminated because there’s more parents unwilling to discipline their children like in the “good old days.” She has this bizarre nostalgia of her childhood’s generation - I was a latch key kid too in ways, if I have kids I’d want them to be independent too, but I don’t think we have to be the sort of parents that are uninvolved in their children’s lives like ours were. 

She doesn’t seem to realize that all of us who did grow up in collectivist cultures also suffer from a lot of mental health issues. Her dismissal of BLM and other movements as being supported by children because they lack parental authority was ludicrous amongst other political assertions made. She seems to be anti-trans and in those moments sounded like an opinionated mom wanting others to agree with her rather than a researcher trying to show their evidence. I tend to roll my eyes anytime anyone quotes Rob Henderson, who she is a huge fan of, he once blocked me on Twitter for asking him a question so don’t think he’s the right person to go to for questions on resilience lol. After recently reading Crime Fictions, on how Black children have been falsely incarcerated, the idea that Black children in America are not psychologically impacted by racism is ridiculous. For these reasons I’ve removed a few stars. I would not recommend my friends to read this book, I’d rather tell them what I learned from it and have a discussion in person on it. 

I might update this review later bc there’s a lot I’m thinking about right now

title: The Information: A History, a Theory, a Flood
author: James Gleick
review:
I actually DNF but because of the effort I put in this book I decided to add it to my 2026 read books. 

Imagine taking the famous Shakesperean line “a rose by any other name would smell as sweet ” and dissecting it in every single possible way. From the characters that come together, to the sounds that form together, to the actual meaning of the phrase as to whether a rose can be represented in any other information, to the computer bits that connected together to show this sentence on your screen. Starting off with language that is produced by drumming to every single other way we convey or create meaning, and how that creation of meaning through language shifts how we conceive of our world. It’s hard to explain but what was life like before the existence of the written word? 

I kind of wish I didn’t read this book, solely because I’m the kind of person who when I learn something interesting I really want to share it with someone. This is the kind of book that will likely get you shoved in your high school locker if you share out loud, unless your friends are all linguists or high. Or I imagine this is the kind of book the students in Dead Poets Society would love to discuss in class. Alas, I’m no longer a student, I’ll have to keep it within myself. 

I really enjoyed the first 25% of the book when it came to the idea of information and how writing literally changed our brains. I’m not sure how much I believe the author there but it was compelling to think about. I enjoyed less when information was reduced to math and data. I lost interest very quickly then, not that math isn’t interesting, but the deep dive into these individual discoveries wasn’t for me. Perhaps if I were still in college I’d find it fascinating. Towards the end I found myself skimming and even skipping sections bc my Libby app kept notifying me that someone was waiting for it. My goal was to finish it today (the due date) but alas I gave up.

about.description: A history of information from talking drums and telegraphs to Shannon's theory and the modern data deluge.

title: Between Two Fires
author: Christopher Buehlman
review:
I’m so glad this is over

I really disliked his depiction of humans with very one-dimensional character arcs, especially of women. I think from an emotional development arc this was on par to that live action tv show Hercules. In fact, I think this would have better serviced as some action series that gets an average rating of 6 or 7 on IMDb but it has loyal fans because the action scenes are interesting to watch, and you can place the show in the background while you cook or do some other house chore. 

I especially disliked the overused character arc where the broody man who has trauma he refuses to deal with is suddenly transformed by an innocent girl whose innocence awakens something in him. I won’t spoil the book, but even the ending annoyed me when the girl mentions why she did what she did. Women are not tools for men's emotional healing, and I don't understand why men think this is normal, it's dehumanizing, as if we were 'created by Adam's rib' to be another organ for his use. 

I am not Christian so uncertain if these concepts of wars between angels and demons is part of the theology or was a fantasy embellishment added for the story, but it felt like the exploration of religion was done poorly. It seems the author may be agnostic or is fascinated as to how religion is adopted in practice, so he wrote from a certain perspective rather than one deeply involved in theological debate/academia. I think a more fascinating exploration of the effect on religion on humans was done by a tv show called Messiah, where this man suddenly appears being able to perform miracles and it affects the population around him. I feel the author was trying to invite us to ask the questions that the show Messiah tried to ask of us, but instead focused on bleak action scenes.

title: Crime Fictions: How Racist Lies Built a System of Mass Wrongful Conviction

review:
“I’m the Blue Power Ranger. I’m going to fight for you” - Andre who created the Power Ranger dream legal team for a terrified 8 year old boy, upon seeing that the Chicago Police Department fabricated a story accusing children of rape and murder. Children who don’t know what a lawyer is, and cry for their mamas, denied that because the rule of law is to request for a lawyer. 

I cried several times reading this book thinking about terrified babies and the monstrosity of the Chicago Police Department, meant to be those who protect but are the perpetrators of violence and extreme trauma. The term white supremacy is not strong enough to describe the pure evil of the actions of the police in falsely incriminating Black children to settle cases. The author at one point describes the police as a “modern day slave patrol” to describe the atrocities the police commit against Black communities in Chicago. 

I’ve read ACAB books such as The End of Policing, but this book that puts you inside the story of innocent children being incarcerated by torturing them, forcing false confessions, hiding evidence of their innocence, and terrorizing them after they are found innocent puts a whole new meaning to ACAB.

title: How to Blow Up a Pipeline
author: Andreas Malm
review:
The manifesto is divided into three chapters, the first was the one in which I felt I learned the most. The first chapter is on how violence has been an imperative in bringing about change - from abolition to the civil rights movement - violence brought about real change. I had no idea that the suffragists focused on violent property damage to acquire the right to vote! Especially through arson, while having zero casualties. Andreas denounces moral pacifism in a convincing argument (enjoyed reading even if you already agreed with this remark) by noting that pacifism results in surrendering to suffering and atrocity. Gandhi apparently went so far as to write in an open letter addressed to the Jews to voluntarily suffer in response to genocidal anti-semitism?!? 

The second chapter is on how to stop living in denial of the atrocities against the climate, and focuses particularly on how the ultra wealthy are responsible for putting us in this position. Andreas’s goal is for consumerism & luxury to be removed from being the norm. 

The third chapter is against those who express despair against climate action because it’s too late. 

I wish I had bought this book instead of ordered it from the library because I can see myself reading passages from this book again because the way the author puts ideas together & crafts sentences is worth remembering and revisiting.

title: Of Loss and Lavender: A Novel
author: Sinan Antoon
review:
A tragic, poetic novel about two different Iraqis of two different generations coming to America, living lives that seem are unrelated to one another until the ending. One had his ear cut off by the Iraqi government for refusing military service, the elder is a retired physician suffering from dementia wishing to return to his home in Baghdad. 

The depiction of both the terrifying difficulty of living in Iraq under Saddam to the reality of being a brown man in post 9/11 America is really well psychologically depicted through these two different perspectives.

The author did an incredible job depicting the emotional nuances of the main characters along with other Iraqis that they loved or had to respond to - from the wealthy American Iraqis who ignore the traumas to those abroad, to the women they loved back home. I found the author having caricaturistic depictions of the women in America, especially those who had a romantic relationship with Omar. I honestly don’t understand why any of those women would be want to be in a relationship with him, it’s like these women just appeared out of nowhere for the sole purpose of being romantically involved with Omar. Although I deeply empathize with Omar, I don’t think it excuses his very selfish behavior with the women he uses - honestly reminded me of the tropes we brown women complain about brown men - like please go to therapy or figure it out before you involve us in your complex life that you’re not willing to face. Anyway, just my one opinion that has nothing to do with how I rated the book - Omar is unlikable though still very easy to feel sorrow for which really depicts the talents of the author. 

Warning: There are graphic depictions of torture that were hard to stomach as you knew this really happened.

title: Autocracy, Inc.
author: Anne Applebaum
review:
This is very clearly xenophobic, pink-washing, hawkish, military-stock-owning neoliberal propaganda. I’ve lost any sense of respect for the Pulitzer Prize based on the utter bullshit this book is. I kept thinking of Malcolm X’s, “The white liberal is the worst enemy to America” where he goes on to distinguish the white liberal from the white conservative - the conservative is at least openly hostile, while the liberal presents as an ally while managing, diluting, and containing Black liberation. The relevance here is that the book’s “liberal pro-democracy” posture decides which forms of authoritarianism count as evil and which ones get absorbed into the story of American virtue. If you don't believe this is propaganda, just count how many times she used words like 'anti-americanism' and in what context. 

The sheer audacity of this book is remarkable. Applebaum makes fun of a media outlets like Yalla which she says is funded by RT, but makes no mention of the American media conglomerate, where media monopolies are being held up to ensure billionaire propaganda is spouted on all news networks. title: Bad Company: Private Equity and the Death of the American Dream
author: Megan Greenwell
review:
Last week I ran into someone who mentioned they work in PE, I joked I was reading a book on how PE is robbing the world. They smiled and joked back, “Someone’s got to fight from the inside.” There’s no fighting from the inside. Private equity is an evil born out of Milton Friedman’s idea that a corporations only goal is to maximize profit, one in which anything else -solving someone’s problem, avoiding pollution, employee benefits and rights, etc - is shrugged off as socialism. Friedman’s thesis destroyed much of what makes life worth living - companies now make an absurdly large amount of money through financialization rather than selling actual products. This means that the wealthiest are busy finding different loopholes in the financial world, loopholes the rest of us don’t understand, to squeeze as much money as possible out of anything and anyone with little care to the consequences. 

The book, similar to one I read earlier called “There is no place for us,” follows four different people whose lives and communities are dramatically destroyed by private equity. We follow a dedicated of Toys R Us employee whose life was uprooted by the companies bankruptcy through PE practices, a physician whose local rural hospital became a joke in terms of providing care, an organizer whose housing insecure neighbors are stuck with a landlord who ignores the most nightmarish living conditions, and a passionate journalist who moves from newspaper to newspaper watching her industry shrink through PE scheming. 

One of the reasons why it seems like we can’t do anything about PE? $42 million is spent by PE lobbyists on elections, Senator Schumer himself receive $1.2M from these lobbyists one year. Mitt Romney famously was CEO of Bain Capital, and his polite demeanor distracted us from the reality that his actions cost jobs. 88% of pension funds invest in PE, making it seem like like they’re untouchable. And most importantly, most of us, including myself, don’t really understand how PE works and so ignorance becomes a difficult issue to organize people into action. 

This books was rage-inducing, I found my jaw dropping at certain parts such as PE buying up lots of mobile homes to increase the rent on those whose lives depend on having access to parks. PE is a completely soulless, demonic industry set to do whatever it can to make money. 

And yet, in all four stories we see that communities gathered to fight back. Rarely does a book, especially a non-fiction book make me cry, I found myself shivering and tearing up in the last section, amazed at the power of community passion. I believe this book should turn into a movie or documentary for it’s a powerful tale of David vs Goliath, where David is large groups of people being harmed by private equity realizing it’s time to fight back. 

One thing I wish I could learn is what can we do to share the reality of PE? How do we make it so toxic to be associated with politicians feel the pressure to stand up against them? How do we show people learning about how PE operates isn’t as scary as we’d think it’d be?

title: Between Two Rivers: Ancient Mesopotamia and the Birth of History
author: Moudhy Al-Rashid
review:
When I was in college I took a few ancient history classes with an elderly professor who looked like he could play a stereotype of a historian archeologist in Indiana Jones. He spoke monotonously, had an austere personality that required the entire class to stay in silence, and erudition that was unquestionable. Moudhy Al-Rashid challenged my image of the untouchably serious historian. She made me laugh out loud with anecdotes from her own life, openly admitted that even academics get bored reading ancient tablets, and wore her fascination with Mesopotamia so joyfully that I finished the book wishing I could be her best friend. One of my favorite lines in the book was wrapped in parentheses on anti Iraq war protests: “I was one of those protestors at Columbia University’s quad alongside hundreds of others who opposed the invasion, including a friend who held up a cardboard sign that read, “My bush would make a better president.””

I have had an amateur interest in ancient history nearly all my life, and to this day will watch YouTube videos clearly created by creators whose only goal is to maximize profit. Al-Rashid was quite different in the lessons, books, and videos I’ve watched in that she steers completely away from the Great Man Theory of history. What distinguishes Al-Rashid from most popular history is that she consistently refuses to let Mesopotamia become an abstraction. Rather than centering kings, wars, and shifting borders, she repeatedly asks what history looked like for the enslaved, women, children, scribes, and other ordinary people. You could clearly imagine what society was like for the average person in Mesopotamia, instead of hearing it from above looking at how maps and boundaries were redrawn due to the proclivities of men and their desire for power. It was a completely different way of looking at history, it made me realize that perhaps before this I understood ancient history in a similar way David Attenborough depicts animals - all they do is eat, sleep, compete for dominance and reproduce -  and that’s all they were programmed to do. Because this history was thousands of years ago, and because we’re taught it from a systematic or great man hero perspective we lose sight of the idea that they were humans just like us. 

Some things I enjoyed reading about :

- How she looked at school tablets to understand what the priorities are of the societies. She also brought up this shocking fact that children were learning what is the Pythagorean theorem a milennia before Pythagorus existed!
- How astrology was viewed as a science just like astronomy. Astronomy is observing data points of the skies to predict the mechanics of what will happen in the heavens. Astrology was exploring the same data points to predict what was going to happen on earth. Imagine we know today that the moon affects the waves, the sun determines growth of plants, so why wouldn’t the ancient observe other data to see what else in the skies affect us? The data captured here made way for mathematical astronomy.
- The complicated way to understand slavery in the past. It’s not all chattel slavery as we know of it. One of my favorite parts was reading about a woman who became free, and the next thing she did was go to court to fight for the freedom of her children. One of the Sumerian words for manumission translates to “return of the mother” and today is used as a phrase to mean “freedom” in Iraqi protest art

Overall really enjoyed the takeaways from this book even though the first few chapters were a little boring for me. I closed the book wondering whether Mesopotamia would occupy the same place in our cultural imagination as Egypt, Greece, and Rome had Iraq not endured decades of war and instability.

title: The Qur'an The Great War And The West
author: Imran N. Hosein
review:
I… don’t know 

Last night i took a class where the discussion was on one of the chapters of the Quran related to protection from magic. I left wondering what do I actually believe about magic and what it can do? Surah Falaq and Surah Nas are two of the most repeated surahs as they are the last chapters of the Quran, why are they last, and do we really need to protect ourselves from this? 

I ended up going down a rabbit hole internally about what I believe in that isn’t based off of Western rationality, and then thought of one of my childhood favorite subjects - Islamic eschatology. Someone had recommended this scholar to me and I found him online with some interesting thoughts such as how the fall of Constantinople does not fulfill the prophetic prophecy because the way the Ottomans did it was not through an ethical lens - we are supposed to be allied with Christians not against them. It made me wonder - haven’t political entities that are Christian based  seen us as the “other” enemy for centuries - from the Crusades to Columbus sailing to the west to defeat the Muslims - it doesn’t feel like we’ve been allies.

Another thing he mentioned was King Faisal’s greatest mistake was to trade oil in USD, claiming it was one of Kissinger’s foulest schemes. He then talks about how BRICs is one of the greatest threats to the western economy and will be the reason for its downfall. 

The Great War is, according to him, coming soon and using primarily the Quran he predicts this. I was fascinated by this because most scholars I’ve read on eschatological works focus on the Hadith, but he uses the Quran mostly to defend his beliefs. I never really thought of the Quran as being the source of how the world ends, moreso the Hadith, so that was the pull. 

I’m not convinced of his arguments, but I also don’t think I can toss the entire book out. 

I’ve long had this arrogant belief that I’m not gonna read any Islamic books with badly made covers because theyre likely an indication that the scholar who wrote them isn’t the kind I’d want to listen to. I don’t think I found evidence against this hypothesis, but, I’m still curious about what I think will happen. Nuclear war does feel like something we may witness in our lifetime, who do we listen to? The west is losing its image as being the ones who defend ethics and justice, so who do we listen to?

title: Love & Other Monsters
author: Emily Franklin
review:
Love & Other Monsters is an aptly titled novel of historical fiction giving voice to the forgotten stepsister of Mary Shelley during the summer she writes Frankenstein. Claire is an innocent, vibrant teenage girl who lives in the shadow of the famous authors around her. Both her stepsister and brother-in-law are celebrated writers who treat Claire with patronizing affection. They see her as not a "real" author, and yet she's brilliant in her own way of understanding how the world works - except in one area - love.

Emily Franklin does a brilliant job portraying a teenage girl falling in love for the first time, whose love is built simply on the fact that a man she respects chooses to pay attention to her. Lord Byron, a decade older, takes advantage of her naïveté, playing with her heart. I recently watched a video discussing the difference between how girls and boys are raised - girls spend so much time thinking about love in its various forms, with the apex being loved by a man, while boys are taught to pursue their professional dreams, with love as a side project. Claire, in the romantic wiles of a teenage girl, is completely enveloped by her love for Lord Byron, and the tragedy of what will happen is told through her own first-person narration—a tragedy the audience unfortunately understands long before she does. Claire's teenage devotion to a man is deeply relatable, for we are propagandized to seek the affection of men, even when they are mediocre or deplorable in the affection they return. Claire's coming of age arrives too late. She realizes she is above men only shortly before discovering she is pregnant with Byron's child.

All the men in this book are losers. Mary Shelley's husband is an exhausting man, constantly in need of attention and of being doted on by women, whom he sees as beneath him. Byron is arrogant, a womanizer, and writes out of a ridiculous need to compete. The people with true discernment are Mary, who writes on her own terms, and Claire, who perceives the world clearly even while enraptured by Byron. Meanwhile, the men pompously regale one another with their own thoughts, dismissive of women, while it is the women who produce brilliance. Who remembers any of Byron's work today, and who doesn't know the story of Frankenstein?

Love, in Claire's case, is the monster—a force that harms her life. As we know from history, Byron takes their child and does not allow Claire to see her daughter. Claire and Mary are caught in a world owned by men, learning to survive within it despite both possessing strikingly feminist instincts, especially for their time.

> "To be a woman in the world was to make sense of men's words."

> "Men do not change, they merely unmask themselves."

> "How we look to others to be the answer, when in truth they are the questions we ought to ask ourselves." Claire realizes she had become completely besotted by Byron, hoping he would provide her with security, only to discover—too late—that true security must come from within.

> "You cannot possibly know what it is to live your life constantly underestimated." - A sad sigh at the enduring reality of women living in a world so often governed by mediocre men.

The book is a convincing argument against making a man the center of a woman's life. Claire's greatest mistake is believing that fulfillment will come through a man who is incapable of loving her as she deserves. Reading it in 2026, it feels timely. As more women are able to support themselves financially and exercise greater control over their futures, many are asking a question that Claire herself never had the freedom to ask - What place should men occupy in our lives? If the novel offers an answer, it is that the deepest, most enduring forms of care come not from Byron's passion but from the women who continue to protect, understand, and sustain one another.

review:
I saw a review of this book on an online Islamic magazine, but could not find a copy as it seems this is out of print. Somehow, I ended up finding this short story read out loud by Lavar Burton, who has a podcast where he reads his favorite short stories. It was delightful to have the man behind one of my favorite childhood shows, Reading Rainbow, reading a book which involves him saying out loud praises of Allah. That alone made this a wonderful listen, though I don’t really listen to audiobooks and had to rewind a few times to catch what was said. 

The story is a time travel story through the lens of Islamic wisdom. Was shocked to learn the author is an atheist as his way of understanding the lessons of the Quran and how Arab fables were written was astonishing. The story involves principles like Qadr, Divine Mercy, and Repentance. 

I felt like it was a -coincidence- that I ended up seeing this article yesterday, because I’m taking a class on Surah Yusuf, which the Quran calls the most beautiful story and it is entirely about how God Plans in ways we can’t comprehend, how the reward for good is only good, how Allah is Ar Rahman, and the importance of repentance as a way to mend what was broken. All of these are themes in the stories we hear as the main character learns from the alchemist different characters who used to the time travel machine. 

I really loved this because sometimes I feel like the Quran is too idealistic (as a Muslim probably heretical for me to say this) and I struggle with the concepts Allah calls us to. And yet, it is true - when we approach our actions with the right intentions - mercy, repentance - then what is the reward but goodness? And if we approach our actions with the wrong intentions then what is the result but an opening to a pathway to repent? And will we take that path?

title: How Soccer Explains the World
author: Franklin Foer
review:
I think I would love the same concept of this book written by someone who isn’t American, literally someone from anywhere else in the world. Perhaps, Iran given their absurd circumstances they had to deal with in the current World Cup, Senegal based on the history of racism they have dealt with directly in an infamous Morocco match, Brazil because of its centrality in the history of World Cup soccer. Like literally anyone else, I almost felt the same frustration I’ve been feeling watching the American commentators speak during live games, where they clearly are ignorant of the existence of any country in the global south, and as a result are extremely unfair to any non European or non American team. This author definitely writes from a more cosmopolitan & learned perspective but I still left quite frustrated. 

For example, the chapter on how soccer explains Islam focused entirely on Iran decades ago. The author concludes that globalization will have a negative impact on Islam, based on policies that Iran implemented, and yet corrects himself at the end with a tiny paragraph pointing out how other countries are doing. 

I also was frustrated with his writing style, where he inserted himself in almost every chapter, when what was interesting was the discussion on private equity, racism, political realities that affect how soccer is viewed, and other politics. I felt like I didn’t learn enough about any of this, and part of it was the bizarre organization inside the chapters.

I was fascinated by the idea of the uber wealthy buying and trading Black and brown players, as it felt like the vestiges of slavery or human trafficking. The chapter on the Serbian team being actively involved in genocide was also something I’ll remember for a long time.  The author also kept bringing up Naomi Klein which made it seem like he has a progressive view on things, but I left feeling like this author doesn’t really fully grasp what he’s writing. 

Anyway, I want to read this book again, just have it not written by an American.

title: The Great Mental Models: General Thinking Concepts
author: Shane Parrish
review:
Found myself wondering why I’m reading a common sense book for about 2/3rds of the book, which reads like long flash cards of mental models. The book’s audience is likely those who want to learn more on critical thinking but if you’re in strategy or engineering work a lot of this will be an I already know this.

 The last third I found more interesting and there was one mental model I learned for the first time - Hanlon’s Razor - which says rather than assuming malice, assume the person is making a mistake or choosing the laziest option. Rather than assuming people are out to get you, see that they’re making an “easy” choice. I really liked this as it’s a direct counter to cynicism or misanthropy, which based on this mental model says it’s a way to end up making really bad decisions. Been feeling a bit cynical lately so this felt like a good shot of let’s not go down that path. 

Personally think you can use this book as an ingredient list for making any sort of self help book. Just pick a few, find a bunch of examples and voila you got a best selling book. 

I think I may read his next volumes because this one felt like an intro, perhaps the next ones get into more complexity.

title: Starling House
author: Alix E. Harrow
review:
I happened to be staying in an old Victorian home turned B&B that once I sent a picture to my mom she told me to pray since she was convinced it’s a jinn hot spot, so I C decided to read a book about an old Gothic haunted house while there. I think I was silly for picking up this book from BookTok, knowing that BookTok likes romantic fantasy, without thinking this was a romance book. 

I really enjoyed the setup of this book, a housing insecure woman who lives in a way where she is ignored for her poverty but is trying to scrap by with a minimum wage job that only allows her 30 hours so the store doesn’t have to pay her health insurance - she’s cynical for good reason, protective of her teenage brother, smart in knowing how to navigate life through forgeries/petty theft/trickeries. She wants really badly to save money so her little brother, who she is responsible for as her mother is dead and the father has long ago left, so as to give him the life she doesn’t have the opportunity to have. Opal believes that people in her situation don’t get to dream, but she dreams for her brother. In comes Starling House, a house with many different stories from the town, and one she is constantly drawn to. It’s a house that is occupied but no one ever sees the resident, anyone going in or out, and it’s known to be the epicenter of bad things happening in this small Kentucky town. One day the door opens and she finds herself employed by the houses owner as a housekeeper, with the wage that would give her the opportunity to give her brother that dream.

I enjoyed the anti-capitalistic framework through the lens of Elizabeth Baine who is a consultant for a mysterious company that will do nearly anything for its clients, and that includes harassing a woman who lives in a motel with her brother. I also enjoyed hints to Kentucky history with its minor references to Black history in the region. I found her writing to be beautiful. But once the actual romantic fantasy started I found myself wanting to finish it, because I felt the romance made the story a lot less interesting.

title: There Are Rivers in the Sky
author: Elif Shafak
review:
This book felt like reading a love letter on the tragic history of Mesopotamia/Iraq, through an oppressed group, the Yazidis, who may have roots to the ancient Assyrian empire. But it was clear that the one writing the letter is not rooted in the culture or history of Mesopotamia/Iraq, as much of the book felt like they were explaining a people, culture, and history they themselves were actively learning. Having loved Elif Shafak’s other historical fiction books, this is where I realized her talent really lies in writing about what she knows - the complexity of practice and history of Islam - as her other historical fiction books detail with. 

Oddly, my favorite character was the Orientalist, Arthur, who grew up in poverty and through his love of ancient history finds his way to Nineveh, making discoveries that bring Iraq to the forefront of history. His pursuit of knowledge without consideration of the politics or philosophy has dire consequences on who gets to own and define history. Arthur, in his journey, slowly learns the lack of ethics in his actions, but being that he only is able to understand the world through his European lens he never has the ability to really articulate why. His “exotic” love interest reminded me a lot of the longing story of Layla & Majnun… and well I guess the author knew that. 

With Narin’s story, I thought of my Kurdish friends, who have shared stories of families escaping Saddam by going up the mountains, absolutely terrified that the only way out is up. The atrocities of the Yazidis are really made clear through the genocides they experience, through being seen through prejudiced eyes, through being unheard. 

One reason this book was interesting to me is that at the beginning of my studies I wanted to focus on ancient history. I took classes on Ancient Greece, Egypt, and Rome, daydreaming of being able to one day really tell the stories of the prophets. The history of Mesopotamia is usually long forgotten in ancient history classes - perhaps because of the atrocities that have occurred in Iraq. You would think that Iraq, hosting several prophets, including Prophet Yunus, as mentioned in the book, having the Ziggarat of Ur - related to Prophet Ibrahim,  supposed tower of Babylon, the Code of Hammurabi, and more would make this one of the top visited countries in the world for lovers of how human civilization unfolded. People flock to Greece, Italy, Egypt, Palestine  and other places throughout the Middle East, but ask somebody if they’ve visited Ur, and people won’t know where it is on the map. It doesn’t make any sense, and perhaps this brings me back to the first sentence of the review, this felt like a romantic lament of the tragedy of Mesopotamia & Iraq. 

The book made me think a lot about how history is memorialized, how politics shapes it, who gets to decide what is important in history, and how we are all weaved together in those decisions. 

The reason I’m giving it 3 stars is it took me a really long time to get into the book, I kept dragging it along with me, and I think the relations between the characters is not that well made. However, because I think the book is really about how history is weaved together into a story, it makes sense that they seen unrelated.

title: Taboo: A Ph. D. Girl in the Red Light Area
author: Fouzia Saeed
review:
Read this book many years ago, and ended up thinking about it this morning. The book involves a researcher studying the red light district in Lahore, a district so large it has its own representatives in government. She explains how sex work operates in a Muslim country, challenges the assumptions we have made about sex work, and expresses how those with power utilize and keep the place functioning. This book challenged a lot of my assumptions about sex work, but also shares the reality of patriarchy in Pakistan through the lens of this business. One area I remember thinking about for years after was how this can be legalized through mut'ah contracts, it really made me evaluate what nikah contracts really are in Islam, sending me down a rabbit hole of reading papers on nikah contracts & legal perspectives of it throughout history. For instance, I didn't realize until this book that a nikah contract can really be reduced to legalizing sex between two people, as linguistically the word is related to sexual relations & in many cases in Islamic history consummation can determine the fulfillment of the contract. I imagine this book would not be suitable read for today's audience, as perspectives of sex work have dramatically shifted (she used the term prostitution not sex work for instance). 

A companion read to this is Umrao Jaan Ada by Mirza Ruswa, a book turned into one of the most famous Bollywood movies that romanticizes human trafficking through the protaganist. However, the book itself is written from Umrao Jaan's perspective, and provides her agency where she shares a theory about men I have held in the back of my mind to this day - that men want to capture women who captivate them through their intellect, banter/wit, soft skills and then control them. Once they control them, where the woman ends up losing what initially attracted the man to her, they lose interest wanting to move onto the next alluring woman. I remember finding this fascinating as Umrao Jaan was commenting on how the men who would come to her were men who were married to South Asian women with traditional values. It was the first book I read in my teen years that reshaped my idea of how to include men in my life.

title: Wolfish: Wolf, Self, and the Stories We Tell About Fear
author: Erica  Berry
review:
Two weeks ago I watched the horror Obsession, and I have been afraid of men since. The movie is an on the nose metaphor of a “nice guy” who completely destroys a woman, believing he’s the victim the entire time. His selfishness is defended by all those around him, and they feel bad for him, whereas the woman is increasingly isolated for her reaction to his behavior. I left that movie believing men are incapable of love, they’re only able to desire - and they use that as a way to approach women - not capable of being kind or loving to women who they aren’t physically attracted to or biologically related to. That is, all men are predators. They don’t see us inherently of any worth unless we belong to them in some way. 

We’re fed this lie that men are protectors and they will defend women, but in nature often the predators who are defending and caring for their loved ones are mothers. What is the purpose of men then?

“Traditionally, white men’s defense of white women’s bodies has been less about inherent respect and more about the maintenance of alleged property… the white damsel is valuable to the white man not just because she is “his” but because she, in her constructed victimhood, supports his rise to hero. Her own power is limited.”

Like in Obsession, the woman exists as mere validation for the man, men everywhere are raised the same. What is horrifying about that movie is that we have been raised to laugh off or to our eyes at male incompetence, generally emotional incompetence. It’s part of life. In an attempt to be understood by a man, I’ve received a meme from Family Guy that says “men, we don’t know what we did” to minimize my concerns. Obsession puts that male incompetence on blast, depicting how that results in violence of the woman. 

This book does something similar, in that, it’s about our fear of wolves, and it explores all sorts of expressions we have used today (ex “lone wolf”) to understand why we fear an animal that most of us will never encounter. The online meme about “the woman would choose the bear over the man” is about how bears only attack for their own means, whereas men will harm and be completely apathetic to the harm they created and society will reward them for it. She uses our fear of the wolf to talk about the predator hs women do have to deal with, men, and how we live constantly in fear of men, but we’re minimized as this is just the normal we must accept. She also explores race, and how, she as a white womancan serve both as predator and prey, but for the most part she talks about the feeling of being prey. (I did get annoyed when she mentioned George Zimmerman’s self defense argument, saying she can’t call him a murderer bc the law says he isn’t. The law also said women could vote for over a century). 

She also explores common stories around wolves, especially Little Red Riding Hood, where the little girl keeps asking questions to the wolf and slowly trusts the wolf until he eats her. The warning being that it’s the women’s fault for letting her guard down, we can’t stop the predator from being a predator. Wolves, and in ways, men are naturally like this - and the more dangerous kinds are the ones we learn to trust and let our guard down. It made me think about how I have not identified as a feminist for several years, wanting my mercy to overcome the belief that women are naturally going to be preyed upon by men. By letting that guard down I was harmed a number of times again. The feminism was a shield, a protection against men. The danger of Circe was being merciful to men, poison was the way to protect oneself in a realm where one is forced to look like prey. The lesson is to know at any moment a man may harm or abandon you, a woman on the other hand will nurture. 

I had come into this book thinking it was going to be solely about wolves and the way we fear animals, I left thinking about the concept of predators. And it made me realize that perhaps my growing misandry is a fear response, and perhaps it’s protecting me.

As a Muslim I kept thinking of this Hadith where Allah says that Rahman - the most merciful - comes from rahm - womb - which mostly only women have. I kept thinking about how women’s rahma is what keeps the world going, and I kept thinking of how men have so little of it.

review:
A novel of a Palestinian woman unraveling while, from my limited perspective, running away from her identity and trauma. At first I found the unreliable narrator to be difficult to understand, as it perplexed me why she was so materialistic constantly comparing herself to luxurious brand names and the haves vs. have nots. But by the end it becomes clear that just like everyone else who identifies themselves with luxurious brands, it’s really a way to avoid oneself by hiding behind varying layers of social status, a marker that has no real meaning. She sees herself as above Palestinians who are more identified with their heritage, and uses these Western markers of success to differentiate herself. She has no real connection to anyone around her, her sense of values not existing while trying to believe it does. She finds herself living through her sexuality and class comparisons. 

However, as she becomes more unhinged, and is confronted by people who knew her family back in Palestine, her memories of the land become more real. The complexity of her real identity unfolds, but, unfortunately, it’s at a true mental cost of unraveling in a state that no one will understand. Perhaps that’s why she remains unnamed throughout. 

I don’t know how I feel about this novel but may be attending a book club on this so looking forward to hearing others thoughts.

title: Life After Cars: Freeing Ourselves from the Tyranny of the Automobile
author: Sarah Goodyear
review:
Imagine a life without cars; a life that would be beautiful, communal and environmentally friendly. If someone has never thought negatively about cars and is curious about someone’s anti-car stance this would be the perfect book for them, as it’s easily accessible. However, if you’re someone who spent even an hour hating on cars than this book may be more of a skimmable amalgamation of all the reasons cars are bad for us, where you wouldn’t learn too many new things, but perhaps acquire the confidence to speak against them to your friends. 

Some areas I appreciated the dive into:
- the consideration of children when it comes to urban planning. The reality that by having a car-centric world we are inhibiting their social recreation and individual autonomy, all harming their ability to be independent adults 
- how cars have made us more unethical, angry and dehumanizing of one another, whereas more interaction with people creates more community
- how instead of using the term anarchism to describe ignoring laws and changing things for their own they used the term “tactical urbanism,” which would be a great term for me to use next time I find myself stealing traffic cones to save wildlife 

Things I didn’t like about it:
- the first few chapters feel like they were written by a different author than the rest. Something I wrote after finishing chapter 2 in my notes: “ I feel Like This book is written for the self righteous Brooklyn hipster who already has all the pedantic knowledge of how life should be lived - they’re anti-racist, pro community, pro environment, etc - but they look down on anyone who doesn’t ascribe to these views. So they prefer to stay in their communities of Williamsburg or Bushwick” however, the tone shifted after the first few chapters and I found my annoyance disappear, which, when I finished the book made me wonder which author was responsible for those sections. 
- They mentioned in the chapter on children that urban planning was designed around adults, but what I think they really wanted to say was adults who have corporate jobs. It’s quite clear that the 9-5 soul sucking routine has contributed to this life & getting rid of that would help us live more free lives. Many of us are shackled to our cars because we can’t get paid without it 
- although I appreciated the sections describing how European cities accomplished the impossible of having car free streets, I still couldn’t find myself imagining the same for US except for the city I currently reside in. Having grown up in a small town, I know that many towns are dependent on their fifty foot tall McDonald’s sign that convince drivers to stop by on the highway. Change can happen really quickly so how do we show that it’s possible?
- one of the reasons listed for why people are afraid of a car free life is weather - how are we supposed to use bikes in the middle of a storm? 
- another reason they state against cars is that disabled people are limited from accessing cars - but how are they supposed to use bikes then? They didn’t really explain how car free would work for disabled that currently do feel a dependence on cars 

My stance against cars began over a decade ago when a shaykh shared with me their theory that cars were the worst invention of modern society. He described them as metal isolation boxes that bring more harm than any good. This book is a good pocket book for the why.

title: Progress: How One Idea Built Civilization and Now Threatens to Destroy It
author: Samuel Miller McDonald
review:
Haven’t been this excited to read a book that challenges my conception of how the world came together since I read “The Dawn of Everything.” I judged this book by its cover and when I saw it being compared to Jared Diamond or Yuval Hariri, my expectations were low. Wow,  was I delighted to be proven very wrong. 

The fundamental premise of this book is that progress defined through “energy capture” that takes more than it replaces is resulting in the collapse of our world. The ancient agricultural revolution, where we’re taught that we moved from “hunters and gatherers” to settlers of cultivated land that removed us from our natural state, is the beginning of a dangerous philosophy he calls parasitism. Contrast that with how indigenous cultures existed as stewards of the land, progress is fundamentally destroying us. 

His thesis across revolves around a famous Malcolm X quote he cites at the beginning - is it progress if you simply removed a few inches from the knife in your back?  Indigenous societies created communal cultures that were more egalitarian, free, and more in healthy mutualistic or commensalist human ecologies. In contrast, the parisitic culture starting with the denunding of the environment for the purpose of building large agricultural tracts, moved us into competitive, selfish, mechanistic lives that heralded humans above all of the earth. He creates a story starting from the agricultural revolution to present day on how parasitism evolved into the destructive ideologies & actions of today, where we live in collective delusions that somehow we have progressed but really our lives are made miserable by being forced to work for basic healthcare, being shackled by debt, war & genocide, and more.

The philosophical trajectory he provides is awe inspiring in that he really goes from our natural state in harmony with nature to agricultural revolution to empire building to the mess we’re in today - he somehow talks about everything, everywhere all at once without losing track of the overall thesis on parasitism. I felt like this book was a beautiful soup of a lot of other books I’ve read in the past - including Economics: A User Guide by Ha-Joon Chang, A People’s History, The Dawn Of Everything, anything I’ve read by Jason Hickle, books on environmentalism, and more. I also appreciated that he didn’t make this a book about how capitalism is bad and communism is good, he focused on all the forces that eventually evolved to the capitalistic extractive state we have today, avoiding binaries altogether. 

I did lose him towards the end in terms of solution building - radical solutions that we can implement now?! I want to believe like he does, but it’s hard to. I also got a little put off when he randomly mentioned working to bring unbiased but he clearly has a very strong point of view that he’s seeking to persuade you towards. And last, as a New Yorker, I have a hard time believing that cities are anti-environmental, but perhaps I’m heavily biased here. 

He’s also very anti-religion, seeing it as a tool to manipulate the masses, and most specifically against Abrahamic religions. As a Muslim, was surprised to see that the part against the Islamic golden age was mostly focused on the writings of Ibn Khaldun. Just like Western civilization, the Islamic civilization has hundreds of years of philosophical knowledge building, Ibn Khaldun doesn’t represent all of it. In fact in today’s world, one of the most respected Islamic knowledge institutions is indigenous knowledge preserved in West Africa 

And personally on a religious level - if I could talk solely to the author - I was thinking about my religion throughout reading this - Muslims don’t view this world as a waste of time to get to the next world. The average practicing American muslim would say that we are here to be vicegerents, stewards, of the earth - as that’s what God has commanded us to do. And part of figuring out what to do isn’t limited to religious law, but accessing what we call fitra - our natural disposition that is meant to be in harmony with all of God’s creation. We are supposed to have a mutualistic approach to “energy capture.” There’s two famous quotes I was thinking throughout reading this. The first directly from the Quran is a well known verse that the average practicing Muslim would have heard of “we have made you into nations & tribes so you may get to know one another.” This goes entirely against the teleological argument the author argues our religion has, in that the Quran directly acknowledges both nations and nomadic life. In fact when we learn the s history of the Prophet in Sunday School, every child is taught that the Prophet spent his childhood amongst nomads and the significance of that was to move his heart away from the corruption of urban life. The second quote I was thinking about was this quote from the Prophet himself where he says that if the world were ending, if a tree sapling was in your hand you should plant it. Even if everything is bleak we are asked to do what we can to protect all of God’s creation.

title: There Is No Place for Us: Working and Homeless in America
author: Brian Goldstone
review:
I found an anarchist bookstore where the founder started talking to me about housing justice. The complexity of the laws were going over my head so I asked for recommendations & he pulled out a few books. I left this book horrified, enraged, and deeply unsettled that I didn’t know about this reality before, even though I have a shirt from a political campaign emblazoned with “housing is a human right.” A book like this is more convincing of the need to become a socialist over anything Marx has written. 

Following five families, mostly through the eyes of the mother, we are witnesses to the lived reality, terror, prejudice, and deeply systemic injustice of housing insecurity. We see how private equity has transformed the housing market into one that doesn’t see the human in the person seeking housing, how the rich are able to convince those in power to secure more rights for themselves at the expense of the lives of the poor, how exploitive businesses (propped up by PE) take advantage of the vulnerable through tactics of fear/prejudice/blame all through the eyes of the people directly impacted. It’s absolutely absurd how many are profiting heavily from the exploitation of the housing insecure. Tenant organizing is difficult because access to secure housing is such a crucial aspect of livelihood, not having it results in not having the capacity to fight for rights, meanwhile the ex governor of Georgia can open a homeless shelter while oppressing residents of extended stays he co-owns. Having emphatic hearts is nowhere near enough, I realized why we need to actively fight for housing to be a fundamental right of existence. 

We follow the lives of mothers, and it is really hard to see the decisions they are forced to make, with the lack of support from anyone - many of the men in their lives disappear. I also kept thinking of the children, and, how constantly trying to feel at home in places that do not want or care for you can impact their growth & pursuit of education or happiness. All in all this book opened my eyes in a way that they won’t be able to close again. 

Last, as the United States approaches its 250th anniversary, I found myself wondering what it means to celebrate a nation that treats housing as a commodity (see 2008 financial crisis built entirely on the ultra rich trading the poors housing debt) before it treats it as a human need.

The question I’m left with: how do we push for good social housing?

title: Pym

review:
I’ve been on a reading binge trying to find something that I genuinely want to read - I usually read out of curiosity - but what to do when you’re facing a crisis of identity? None of my usual genres for books are tickling my fancy, so I’ve taken up everyone’s recommendations - from friends/family, to good read algorithms, to strangers I meet, to authors. I only read this because I saw the author of another book I recently read review it. 

If I were in a place of curiosity, this book would have sparked my interest for its questions on the (intellectual)  stories we tell ourselves about race, civilization, and the arrogance of the self in processing itself within these ideas. Instead, because of where I am, where I’m trying to remember who I am, this was a swashbuckling fever dream of a story of a curious, funny in an absurd way, highly educated man who thinks he understands reality through his research on race, who ends up confounded by everything around him. Forced to confront his (non)-understanding of reality through the increasing satirical, escalating what-the-f*** is happening plot, that repeatedly dismantles every certainty he begins with, we see that there’s no point in trying to be the hero or victim of your own story. You gotta just live with the madness that is life.

title: Bad Friend: How Women Revolutionized Modern Friendship
author: Tiffany Watt Smith
review:
Wow, this may be the first non-fiction book I devoured in a single day. The kind where I probably will tell the next few people I meet that I read this and attempt to convince that they should read it too. What makes this book super interesting is it's written by a Professor of Emotions, where she understands how emotions are influenced by politics, history, and sociology. 

The title of the book infers that the book is about what makes one a bad friend, but really, the entire book is exploring how we have this fantasy concept, influenced by media (shows like Friends, WandaVision, basically any movie/tv show that includes two female friends) as much as it is about our inability to talk about issues in our friendships, of being or having the perfect, effortless, idealized friend. We look at others and wonder why they seem to have perfect friendships, and we are secretly struggling to define what is happening between us and this other person we love. What I love about this book through her personal narrative as well as her very thorough research is that we all have these insecurities about friendship. 

She explores all sorts of friendships - from teenagers to those close to death, to neighbors to mom buddies, to trying to understand what closeness means to not close, to friends created through poverty to those of the wealthiest, to friendships defined by power imbalance to those where becoming too-merged causes issues of identity collapse, to capitalism affecting our understanding of work friends to 13th century female communes. And also, she gently talks about AI Friends and what the consequences of them are. 

What is most interesting is what happens in the 20th century, where the idea of female friendship surges to a heralded activity (where previously for centuries it was distrusted) - where friendships changed as women entered the workforce. Along with that definitions of 'toxic friends' started to emerge, a label built off of our society becoming more individualized - changing from we 'find friends' serendiptously to we 'choose friends' to optimize our life. What she shows is that by creating definitions around toxic friends we are becoming "more intolerant of human failures in platonic friendships & peddling a myth of a perfect friend" - someone who is immune to life complexities - someone closer to an AI friend! In order to maintain friendships we need to live with ambivalence, the uncertanties that come with major life changes in one of ours or both of our relationships, and demonstrate willingness to work through difficulties. 

She talks about how in her research and examining her own friendships, it's really difficult for people to open up about the difficulties of friendship, since we keep assuming this imagined reality that it's all easy and effortless. But what I absolutely love love love love about this book is how she really describes in 300+ pages that we are all imperfect human beings, we all have no idea how to define things or whether things should be defined, we are all figuring things out, and this idea of fearing being a 'bad friend' is really part of the process of figuring out our relationships with one another. 

This is the kind of book I wish my younger self could have read, and, I know this is the kind not everyone will enjoy based on how it's written. But what it did give was comfort in knowing that we are not alone in feeling uncertain, and, in fact, that is part of the process of being friends. I have read a few books on friendship, and this is for my current life, my favorite book. Prior to reading this, I'd have said my favorite book on friendship would be Anam Cara by John o Donahue, where he speaks of friendship in soulmate terms, spiritually beautiful and meaningful. Bad Friend may not have taken a spiritual look at friendship, but I felt spiritually revived in a way, for letting loose on the grip of feeling like I don't know how to be a friend. She concludes her book by saying that we start friendships with trust, gestures of love, and witnessing each other; but where the story of friendship really begins is when it gets difficult. 

"Friendship is not a permanent state one arrives at. It is something we do. It is a process of negotiating our endlessly changing selves, a process of uncertainty and of learning... The women who live in communities together have taught me a very different kind of story about what friendship looks like: a tale not of glossy ideals but of effort and failure, of chances and mistakes, of imperfections and humility, of feeling inexpert but trying anyway."
