title: Love in a F*cked-Up World: How to Build Relationships, Hook Up, and Raise Hell Together
author: Dean Spade
review:
This was an excruciating read, for it forced me to confront how I relate to others in a way no other relationship book has done. It took me several months to read, because I would have to sit back and review all the ways I am contributing to failure in relationships and community. It forced me to stop victimizing myself, and recognize the responsibilities I am neglecting in spaces I am in. My disposition affects the community overall, and I have to carry more responsibility in that. I have to look at the stories I've carried around with me for decades, and how that results in not being able to interact with people in a loving manner that is respectful to what they need. It's the first book that I've read that deeply goes into how you get triggered, what the process of that trigger is, how to understand how deeply rooted that trigger is and how to reevaluate/tackle that trigger so that you can have a healthy relationship.

There's no romance in this book on love, it's straight to seeing ourselves as systems in motion and how to edit your system to show up appropriately in relationships. Spade uses his organizing background to create frameworks around love in relationships, and brings in his theories on how monogamy is part of the capitalistic/racist/unjust system that creates unfair hierarchies.

What Spade does well is the trigger framework in how we get activated in relationships and what to do with that activation. He has several different ways to analyze this, and his goal is to not have you sit in misery about who you are, but really, carefully, how to not activate yourself so it doesn't activate your loved ones. No other book on love I've read has gone this deep into the mechanics of how we fail each other in real time. For that alone, the excruciating read was worth it.

Where I had trouble & why I personally may not be the right audience for this book:

1. The removal of mystery & enchantment of love: Spade's structuralist approach reduces all the ways we interact into systems, as if I could take his book and use it to program characters in a video game. I have read many books on love - philosophy, biology, neuroscience, history, Islamic - and this was the first that removed the mystery and spirituality out of it entirely. Love, in every other framework I've encountered, retains something irreducible and transcendent, and I had a lot of difficulty to see love in a fully systemic/predictable/easy-to-understand-everything-about-ourselves view.  

2. The underlying assumption of plurality & impermanence: Spade's framework assumes that relationships, romantic, friendships, community bonds - - all forms of love - - are naturally fluid. That people come and go, that we shed relationships and begin new ones, and that this movement is not only inevitable but healthy. What I found myself resisting was the underlying acceptance of impermanence as a natural feature of relationships (which may be dumb on my part as I live in NYC :( ). I believe in the weight/transcendence of relationships, that friendships matter across time, that community is built through loyalty and return. I believe that the people we love are not interchangeable or replaceable (which to be fair he also says, but perhaps I couldn't really understand due to the plurality aspect). I believe in family, and the feeling of rootedness, through relationships that carry foundation are vital for our personal wellbeing as well as the wellbeing of overall community. And, yes, I do believe in marriage as a goal, in direct contradiction to what he argues as healthy, though I do agree with his argument on how systems of marriage produce inequity and injustice. Spiritually, I believe every interaction we have with one another will be held to account in the life after death. That we will be with the ones we love in that world. Spade's framework doesn't seem to have room for that kind of permanence. For him, the healthy thing is to move, while, for me, the sacred thing is to stay. Perhaps I am too conservative for this book.

3. His focus on romantic relationships: Throughout the book he repeatedly mention that the over focus on romantic relationships results in us neglecting the importance of friendships and other relationships. He even says that we should prioritize friendships above romantic ones. But then he ended up spending the majority of the time talking about romantic relationships, so I felt like I didn't get the full picture. I also was surprised he didn't really go into family dynamics - but perhaps this book was meant for people who are not interested in family but focusing on less permanent relationships.

title: When Hearing Becomes Listening: Prophetic Listening and How It Can Transform the World Within Us and Around Us
author: Mikaeel Ahmed Smith
review:
A significant portion of what happens on the Day of Judgment is the rights of other humans. The Prophet (S) mentioned 3xs in hadith that character is our religion. Something Sh Mikaeel believes in is that we are here to use our individual gifts, to bring betterment to everyone (which is inclusive of ourselves). We have to care about everyone. How do we do that with our limited capacity?

Iris Murdoch, who I read way back in Philosophy 101, writes, "Love is the extremely difficult realization that something other than oneself is real. Love, and so art and morals, is the discovery of reality." Perhaps the most difficult realization of my life, especially within the last year, is how difficult love can be (not limited to the western concept where they prioritize romantic love). How difficult it is to realize that the other person is real, beyond your desires of them, beyond your distorted perception of them and beyond your own nafs. 

Reviewing the teachings of this book the past two weeks (I read this book last year), I realized how important it is to really get to know myself, beyond social media, beyond the push and pull dynamics of social engineering, beyond the ads, beyond the expectations of others. Who am I? Prior to Ramadan starting this year, I had a major crisis of identity, and now, I am looking to fundamentally build myself back together. Who am I?

Why is this important on a book on empathy - because Prophetic empathy comes with a deeply rooted sense of self. And with that, this past month, I did the exercise Sh Mikaeel offers on creating the different circles of people in your life, and deeply reflected on what this means. As Muslims, our priority is to develop a relationship with Allah (SWT), and with that is having a well-rounded sense of self. Then we have a few people within our inner circle who should make up 70-80% of our interactions and focus outside of our personal circumstances (work, salah, personal time). And then the next circle is the close friends, how much time should we devote to that? And the next circle... and so on and so forth. The importance of this is that with this focus we can create a deep sense of responsibility and rootedness, as human connection is absolutely vital, and then we can use this sense of self & responsibility to love... everyone. 

What is the noise I'm processing my reality with (my triggers, my defense mechanisms, my influences, etc.), and how can I address these so that I can be more present in relationships? This is the fundamental problem Sh Mikaeel is seeking to solve. I originally liked Sh Mikaeel's previous book better, but, after going through the identity crisis, the practical frameworks he provides in this book through an Islamic lens have humbled me into seeing how my vices have made it difficult for me to listen to myself, Allah (SWT), and.... everyone else. And this isn't about recognition, this book can help one actively solve their internal noise so they can really embody what the Prophet (S) taught us.

Imagine there is a day where every single tear we caused to shed will be weighed against us, with that perspective, it becomes imperative to focus on how we can be the ones who heal what is broken. And that starts with ourselves.

review:
As I was reading this novel, I heard a tiny, sad violin playing the entire time with each page turn. The novel is emotionally monochromatic, where the flatness of the narrator's and Laila's depressed feelings stay the same throughout, which made this difficult to read through. I didn't feel interested in Nadir or Laila enough to want to empathize with them, because there was little to no change to emotion. I kept thinking of other novels I read that are filled with very difficult to absorb and tragic scenes like Yaa Gyasi's Homegoing, and how it is possible to explore nuance even if the characters are expressing void in their life. There was just too many tragedies to follow and too much of trying to put in every single possible form of injustice found in New York City into a book to really get a hold of the character as an individual. 

The first half of the book felt like it was over accommodating to people who are not familiar to Arab culture, rather than let readers come in to see the world through the narrator's eyes, we are given every single possible detail that could happen for someone who is Syrian living in NYC. I found this annoying.

I'm probably not the right reader for this book, I felt like I was back in my AP English days feeling intimidated by the writing since I never saw myself as 'good at understanding literature.' The metaphors of the birds went over my head, and I kept wondering how are they finding this many young-ish people who are this deeply interested in ornithology in NYC?

My favorite parts of the book was traveling with the narrator across New York City, having known some of these neighborhoods it was a delight to see the diversity of the city through the narrator's unique perspective and identities.

title: Regarding the Pain of Others
author: Susan Sontag
review:
We live in 1984: War is awful and yet unstoppable, peace is the norm but unattainable. And with that, us, as spectators of war happening abroad, are contributing to nothing but the continuation of war. At least that's what Susan seems to be saying, though she does question her thesis at points. What is the point of watching someone's suffering? I write this while having been sick for an entire week, having the choice to stay away from people to not be witnessed. Those who are photographed in war, as Susan points out, are not named, transformed into symbols for our vouyeristic consumption captured by "specialized tourists" aka journalists.

Importantly, she circles the concept of photography as art, specifically in times of war, a medium that is credentialed as objective and yet always is a personal testimony. How can something be objective and personalized simultaneously, and how does that make it worth our attention? And what does that say about our attention if we erroneously believe that this is objective -or- a personal testimony? Inundated with images of suffering around the world, the end result is that we believe there is too much suffering in the world, and therefore we need to intentionally remove ourselves from consuming the photo.

As I was reading this my mind was mapping ideas elsewhere:
1. The movie Civil War, about two journalists attempting to be 'objective' in their reporting while directly being impacted by the war around them. There's no neutral witnessing of the war from the journalists perspectives, and, yet, they are trained to believe that it is possible. 

2. Presentations I went to in the past year, one just yesterday, by Visualizing Palestine on how data storytelling is an impactful way to help people understand the nuances of apartheid and genocide, along with another by a journalist who founded a company that strategically elevated the content of journalists in Palestine to viral status. Without these strategies, would we be in a place where consciousness of the systematic oppression of Palestinians be so widespread? Would Susan disagree with this - I think yes and a lot of it has to do with how she portrayed Palestine and Israel in her book, which resulted in me knocking this to 4 stars. Would Susan change her perspective on journalists being "specialized tourists" if she could learn that 200+ journalists were deliberately targeted by Israel, and Western media are not allowed to capture the genocide in Gaza? 

3. A trip I went to recently to provide aid to Gaza, part of it required me to visit a refugee camp, where the charity had pushed us to take photographs to showcase home, in an effort to fundraise. I came back from the trip, in my mother's words, 'deeply depressed' and it took me a while to realize that a large part of it was having to fundraise with the intention of being a product to be packaged and sold, while also being told to sell the suffering of others. This is what made me pick up this book in the first place, the book filled in the gaps of how to describe my disgust for the trip, but it didn't provide a clean answer for me to think about in terms of media.

4. I thought about a photographs that have seared into my mind, and one of them is from NYT on reconciliation between Hutus and Tutsis, photographs of victims of the genocide with the perpetrator who massacred their family, and the amount of effort that was done by the government, communities, and individuals to repair. As a voyeur into this image, I cannot imagine reconciliation at this level, and yet there were multiple photos of multiple efforts of reconciliation. 

5. The rise of film photography, just today I saw several young individuals with film cameras interested in using what is the slower process to creating photos. What does it mean for this art to move back to intentionality, rather than constant capture? Is photography the art of "an unexpected event seized in mid-action by an alert photographer" and what does that say about consent, humanization, and avoiding consumption? 

6. I thought a lot about the movement towards abstract expressionism, a movement that was created directly as a result of the atrocity of war, where artists moved into expressing their emotions more than painting realistic portraits. How that may have elevated photography and film, and what that means about art prior to the invention of the camera, where warfare was captured in large mounted frames that one must sit in front of in observation for quite some time to really get a sense of what the artist was depicting. 

7. I think I liked another book I read in college a lot better, "Women as weapons of war: Iraq, sex and the media" - a philosophical book on how our voyeuristic consumption of war media numbs us to war. Related to that is Susan Collins Hunger Games series, a series that was inspired by flipping through channels - watching clips of the Iraq War followed by game shows. 

I'm not entirely sure what I took away from this book, but I am thinking about a lot of related things.

title: Breaking the Habit of Being Yourself: How to Lose Your Mind and Create a New One
author: Joe Dispenza
review:
I feel embarrassed admitting I’m reading this, as all the STEM loving people in my life would roll their eyes & maybe look at me as if I’ve told them astrology is real. But this book is really good. If you take out the quantum “science” and implications for manifestation, this book is probably the most helpful book I have read on rewiring your brain away from thought patterns you don’t want to live with. 

I’ve read all sorts of self-help books, psychology books, Islamic books all for the purpose of figuring out how to save my mind from its relationship ruining habits, and have desperately adopted various practices that somewhat work & then are forgotten when I realize my anxiety is back at full force. 

I’ll be honest, I picked this book up when I’ve exhausted the “socially acceptable scientific ways” to handle myself, but am trying with strategic dignity to address the root issues of my mind. This book is what I personally need at this point. 

You can ignore his science if it’s too weird, what he does provide is an easy way to addressing your thoughts, identifying thought loops that do not help, and, importantly, giving you the confidence to believe that you can think more beautifully & positively. Even though ppl use his book to “manifest” their dreams, it’s really him helping you alter your thoughts - what if instead of paranoia of the worst thing that could happen, what if instead a joyful thing could happen? What if it’s really joyful - how would you feel? With that future orientation that is rooted in hope, you can then start making slow decisions based on that future reality, and let go of the hooks that keep trying to protect you. You just let life happen, and enjoy the ride. So then maybe it’s not energy magic, but a way of letting go the need to predict the outcome & be open to a more positive outcome. 

I’ve noticed that since reading this book I have moments where anxiety is not ruling my every minute, and I feel like I am getting to know myself out of survival mode. I finally remember who I really am, and it’s exciting to see her come back out. I’m not my anxiety, and this book is the first book I’ve read that allows me to truly believe it. 

This is also the first book I’ve read that has me believing I am not my past, I am not the traumatic things that happened, I don’t need to hold onto these to protect myself from threats. I have the capacity to be present and live presently while looking forward to the future. Although I don’t see myself as a victim, I’ve realized through this book I was victimizing myself through my past. 

Here’s to hoping I can build this into a practice that transforms my habits into being a more optimistic, present focused, joyful person.

title: The City and Its Uncertain Walls
author: Haruki Murakami
review:
Literature was my worst class in school so I doubt I actually understood this book, especially since this is the first by this author I’ve read. Less than the plot, the book felt more about the deep exploration of emotions - conscious and unconscious that interrupt our “real life” from playing out “better”. From daydreams, dreams, to obsessive thinking, imaginative storytelling - all of these get in the way of “real life” - but I believe the author was attempting to demonstrate they are just as real and important to what we believe is our present reality. 

I found it odd that pretty much every single character is described to not have that many emotions, and perhaps that was done on purpose to convey the richness of our imaginatory realm. I don’t know this author so felt while I was reading it he would eventually scold us for living too much in our imagination and to focus on our real lived experience. But that scolding never came, and it caused me to reflect on why I felt it would come. When I was younger I’d spend most of my day in daydreams, and felt my life wasted away, so decided to focus on my present reality - punishing the dreamer. 

If there really is a scolding it’s perhaps on the back cover of the book “Truth is not found in fixed stillness, but in ceaseless change and movement. Isn’t this the quintessential core of what stories are all about?” Which isn’t a scolding but a wise note on how we can’t stay in any of the realms for too long.  

I also liked how we saw multiple people interpret the town and what the walls and dream reading meant. Were any of them right? Were they all right? Is the story we choose based on the collected experiences we have - imagined and real? Regardless, I still don’t understand what the separation of body and shadow meant lol.

I appreciated his writing also felt like reading a dream :) simple and yet incomprehensible.

title: End Times: Elites, Counter-Elites, and the Path of Political Disintegration
author: Peter Turchin
review:
The most interesting theory of this book is elite overproduction as a major contributing factor to what ends in revolution or massive crisis. It’s something I have taken away and will pay particular attention as the country I live in is becoming increasingly unstable and feeling like a dam we’re all apprehensively waiting to burst. 

What I don’t understand is that this doesn’t really explain societies that “collapse” and never come back from massive inequality, like Pakistan. Theres elite overproduction there, which he does explain away with the brain drain as many Pakistanis move abroad, but still does not seem to be heading to a full scale revolution (maybe I’ll regret this comment a few years from now?)

The main crux of this book is an advertisement for the authors database that he’s been collecting for the purpose of conducting data science experiments on history to make large abstract predictions about where we’re heading. I tried gaining access to this database as i work in tech and am curious to examine it, but the website seems to be inactive as I never received any sort of indication of access. So unsure why he made this book advertising his database with no expectation that people would be curious to use the data?

review:
One of my trash reads of the year. Got it because everyone is reading it, it reads like fanfiction. For the mood I’m in it’s a good read to get your mind off of things. 

When I was a teenager who thought I’d write a fantasy book one day there used to be fantasy name generators. It felt like the author chose names of people, dragons and places that way & then chose to write a Mr. Darcy inspired fantasy fanfiction. Language & phrases are repetitive and redundant and then the last part of the book gets unnecessarily pornographic. The main character is a Mary Sue - she gets the best dragon, the best power, the best boy, etc - it’s as such hard to root for her or be too invested in her character. Everyone seems to behave the same age regardless of who they are — even the 100 year old dragon seems to act like a petty 20 something year old. The book is predictable at every moment even the surprise at the very end.

 I don’t exactly regret this read because it made me think about why I love fantasy in the first place — as a safer way to comment on political realities in our world. You don’t really get that here. What you do get is Twilight level romance for adults - and that’s completely fair to be into. Sometimes we need a break from depth & I think I needed that when I read this.

review:
I found parts of this book enlightening & beautifully written, I found other parts pedantic without the pedigree to say so (for instance dismissing the actions of farmers when she’s clearly not well versed in farming). 

As someone in health tech the biggest takeaway is how we are taken eastern practices long meant to be deeply enriching inward practices, stole them from the people the west has conquered & treated as inferior to themselves, and are reselling a secularized version for profit that doesn’t do what the original practice intended. This really spoke to me as it’s so obvious to see — her chapter on meditation was one where I wanted to screenshot each and every page. It’s horrible how capitalism is coming for Eastern wisdom, by removing all that created the sacred knowledges & turning it for profit.

Her personal stories interweaved in all of this were really difficult to read but important to understand the complexity of trauma and finding wellness as someone who western wellness is generally not meant for. 

The only reason for the two stars were there were times it felt like she was overreaching her knowledge and extrapolating points presenting them as facts. The mix of personal narrative and non fiction was sometimes hard to untangle, which is probably her intention, but at certain moments it left me wishing I knew if her thoughts were really valid .

title: Healing: Our Path from Mental Illness to Mental Health
author: Thomas Insel
review:
It makes sense why this book is beloved by people in healthcare startups, and why I haven't seen too many reviews by mental health therapists. Insel writes as if he is writing a McKinsey proposition tackling the mental healthcare crisis, something that is validating to healthcare entrepreneurs everywhere - that disruption and/or proper organization through startup methodologies will be key to improving mental healthcare. It's strange to read this in a bear market, where every week another promising health tech startup has announced a significant amount of layoffs. Insel's work is definitely going to be used, as it already has been, as evidence for why a mental healthcare startup is the solution to the mental healthcare crisis.

Simultaneously, as someone who knows personally and works professionally with a number of mental healthcare providers from MDs, PhDs, MSWs and more I have a feeling this book would be received with mixed reactions from each kind of therapist. In one chapter Insel decries the lack of standardization in mental healthcare education, in another he says that a peer with training that doesn't require a degree can be part of the magical solution to mental healthcare. I do see the challenge of mental healthcare misinformation, particularly on social media such as instagram, where popular therapists can share reductionist theories about how the human mind works. This has so far resulted in people in my generation becoming more knowledgeable about attachment theory, but the dependency on explaining mental health state based on attachment theory is worrisome. It's not the only theory and as Insel mentions, it probably is more important to focus on the now rather than what happened when you were growing up. I wish he tackled more about how to remove the idea of mental illness being an identity, but he merely sprinkled the idea.

For anyone who has been reading about the mental healthcare crisis, most of his examples aren't new. They are examples you can read in other books. So I ended up skimming large parts of the book filled with examples, skipping ahead to why he was bringing up this example. I personally fear his entrepreneurial approach to fixing mental healthcare, I don't know if paying to be part of a community is the solution to the lack of community. I also don't know if a McKinsey business plan -- filled with fancy data points/examples but less policy oriented -- is the appropriate way to tackle mental health crisis. But it seems like due to the popularity of this book, it will be the way that it will be tackled by, at minimum, mental health startups. 

I also found some of his writing slightly pretentious, especially when dismissing criticism he personally deemed not scientific. It felt as if he were the arbiter of what 'science' in mental health was, and if anyone disagreed that isn't science - such as criticism against using medication for certain SMIs. This particularly didn't make sense to me, because there are places in the book where he shares that we don't know how a particular medicine/therapy works, but it somehow works. If you don't know how something works, you just know that it does, is that really science?

title: Power Play: Tesla, Elon Musk, and the Bet of the Century
author: Tim Higgins
review:
Great read on the genius, arrogance, and delusion of Musk. From being gifted in recruiting fellow geniuses, to creating a cult like following where lovers of Tesla literally volunteered time to help with sales of the car, to his horrid and asshole behavior. 

The entire time I read this I felt like I was reading a book about a king, who demanded loyalty from his subjects, constantly dueling with nobles who were always at risk of being permanently removed from the kingdom. Musk expects loyalty while being loyal to no one, constantly decries how he’s being treated unfairly while being abusive to everyone around him, enriches himself while claiming factory workers are lying. The author paints an important picture of a megalomaniac, who gets away with all the horrible things he does because so many people believe in what he’s doing. 

The constant sense of urgency, the constant need to raise money because of an unwillingness to admit foolish decisions that negatively impacts all the people who work under him, the whirlwind of drama that makes it difficult to pause and reflect on how much drama one has been through is reminiscent of how it felt living under trumps rules for years, but with someone whose actually intelligent. 

When genius is more important than character, we get incredibly rich influencers like Musk. As I read the book I kept wondering, at some point in American history we invented things as part of a collective American identity. It seems to now have flipped to us worshipping CEOs, and at the altar of disruption, ethics & character are sacrificed.

title: Elon Musk: Tesla, SpaceX, and the Quest for a Fantastic Future
author: Ashlee Vance
review:
The intro of this book is deceiving, here I thought I was getting an interesting journalist take at a popular tech figure along with all the controversies surrounding him. But it’s like those books you think are meant to open your mind, but actually is propaganda meant to convert you to a new religion. The religion being one where Elon Musk is your god. 

The back cover says it all where all the praise is from self-touting Silicon Valley people who stand upon their ivory tower insulting anyone who doesn’t provide immense productivity or “innovation” to feed their capitalistic souls. 

The book is a hagiographic account of Elon Musk, one which makes him appear to be a genius worthy of cult like worship, while dismissing anyone who stood up to him as jealous, stupid, or unworthy of being in his presence. It’s meant to be a book that services a stereotype you didn’t think existed anymore — those Cheetos eating basement video game players who believing inventions should make you the Tony stark. Hell, even RDJ is mentioned in the book praising thr almighty Elon, a man whose genius is so important we must forgive all of his horrific behavior. Who else is the audience when the virginity of one of his girlfriends is mentioned, the fact that the Female president used to mow her lawn was a sign she was different from the typical girl, and the dropping of Elon being a nerd but also playboy kept being drizzled throughout the book?

At some point I had to stop reading because it was so strange to read this story that put him on such a high pedestal, where you had to read the footnotes to read counter points to what Elon has done?! Placing most of the criticism in the footnotes was such a strange choice, but it was clear that this wasn’t really a journalistic inquiry… it was a holy book meant to inspire you to be greedy for success through hard work. With Elon being your prophet and inspiration. 

Honestly don’t know why it has so many high reviews…

title: Why We're Polarized
author: Ezra Klein
review:
In January a news article about a Canadian political scientist made its rounds, where he said America is headed towards a dictatorship by 2030. A few years ago that would be a laughable statement, but now it feels like we’re not doing enough to prevent this reality. I started this book to learn Klein’s perspective on polarization, and left it being in complete fear of our failing institutions. The American belief in its government, Klein showed, is not what we think it is. Those videos we watched as children in school on “checks and balances” and “im just a bill” we’re nothing more than children’s explanations of how our government works. 

The book sent me to a bizarre existential crisis - what the hell is government and how do we even believe in this ridiculousness. So much of the “original” authors of American government was based on 1) believing that Americans would identify more locally than nationally with government and 2) believing that no one would violate basic decorum. 

In the years since forming our government we’ve had a civil war over slavery, genocide of indigenous people, a civil rights movement that is still ongoing, and much more. Klein’s last chapter includes reminding us that Trump is not as bad as the other white supremacists who used to reign in our country. Lol. As a non-white person living in America it freaks me out completely as to how much whitewashing we went through in our high school history/government classes and how little that’s baked in reality. Our institutions are failing because people are taking advantage of it and because we voters are easily manipulated by identity and group politics. The book shows how we’re not really a democracy, how we’re not really well represented, how voters don’t really get what they are seeking… 
—-
Side note: One thing Klein didn’t mention was the effect of technology and how that’s changing government, and I mean tech companies becoming so big they’re as influential as government and don’t seem to care about being fined for inappropriate, illegal, and unethical behavior. One question I have about that is who is actually governing us? 
—-
I woke up today with the current trending article being about Rudy Giuliani costumed on the reality show Masked Singer. America is *complete madness*, and, yet, everyone seems to be playing along. How is it 2021, and politics is still too impolite to talk about? 

Long story short this book convinced me to believe we’re headed towards dictatorship and there’s not much we can do.

title: The Cold Start Problem: How to Start and Scale Network Effects
author: Andrew Chen
review:
This book is most ideal for people, like PMs, who may not have heard of network effects and want to learn the major theories. For people who are familiar with network effects, this book may help with putting vocabulary to things “you kinda already know.” There’s some great practical advice and areas where I took notes to take back with me at work, but this isn’t a step-by-step instructional guide on building network effects, rather a company stage-by-stage guide using case studies of some of the most well known tech companies. It’s a good way to think about product strategy.

I didn’t know when I got this book that the author was one of the early employees at Uber, back when we’d read articles about how often the company would cross the ethical line of business. It’s strange to read an insiders perspective where the unethical effects of extremely aggressive competition is watered down and even romanticized to describe Uber’s war room. At one point he even pleasantly admits that Uber reverse engineered APIs of rivals to get their average ETA, that’s how much he’s willing to admit on paper so it made me wonder how much he “forgot” to include about Ubers aggressive competitive strategies. His way of also dismissing protestors made him come off as completely unaware of society, I.e. the “I’m objective because I’m elitist and above the poor people” problem. 

Anyway, the only other thing I didn’t like about the book was the strange name dropping of people and places (including a restaurant that probably doesn’t share its prices online). I couldn’t tell if he was name dropping or implying that the only way to truly obtain network effects is by knowing people and by being at places.

title: Shaykh Ahmadou Bamba: A Peacemaker for Our Time
author: Michelle R. Kimball
review:
Wow. What a biography. As an American this book completely changes my perspective on what nonviolent resistance is - the book advertises itself as an Islamic biography of someone comparable to Gandhi or MLK of the modern era, but Shaykh Bamba’s trajectory was completely different than what Gandhi or MLK did. 

As a Muslim, I have often read about the need to purify your soul, remove all character defects, and as such you can change the world. Shaykh Ahmadou Bamba’s story shows how theory can become practice. He literally changed the fate and future of Senegal, and has continued to dramatically transform it today. 

I started this year visiting Senegambia, and was so amazed at how tolerant and spiritual the area is. The region does seem to be untouched by the spiritual colonialism that Saudi Arabia is practicing. Shaykh Ahmadou Bamba inspired an entire region to transform Whats around it by transforming what’s inside us. What a read. I feel like every modern Muslim should read this book.

title: American Dirt
author: Jeanine Cummins
review:
The feeling of terror and hopelessness is depicted superbly well on every page. I finished this book feeling despondent about the condition of migrants and doing a lot of research. This book was probably important for me to read, as I don’t personally learn about migrants outside of news. Cummins goal was clearly to make the story of migrants more than two minutes of a CNN blurb, creating humanity out of a news story that many of us who live our life in America never could fathom. She clearly spent the time researching what she could, and cleverly worked in stories of not just the protagonist but everyone the protagonist involves so we can get a nuanced perspective of traveling on La Bestia. 

The problem with this book is that it’s very clearly written by a white person. I, as a Pakistani american, found the dialogue cringeworthy as I don’t expect and people of color to ever speak like how she depicted the characters. At first I thought maybe Lydia was the type of woman of color who sees White/American culture as superior to their own, but over time it became obvious that the author cannot really understand what it’s like to be a person of color. As the story continued, I got the feeling that she was imagining the story of migrants as if her characters were all white. 

And then as it became obvious that she cannot fathom this, it became uncomfortable. I started imagining myself, as a Pakistani American, having only visited the country as a tourist writing a book about the lived reality of a Mexican migrant. It’s ludicrous and would in this day and age feel absolutely inappropriate, potentially even racist. 

I didn’t really read the reviews on this site before reading this book, as I picked this up after someone I admire recommended it to me. Overall, I believe this book is intended for an audience that could never understand why people would abandon everything they knew to make a journey like this, and it accomplished its goal in this area. The book leaves one understanding that as a privileged American I could never comprehend the trauma of someone taking this journey towards safety. 

However, I believe what would have been better is to have read some of the authors she recommends at the end of the book, who would be able to provide an authentic depiction of these traumatizing journeys to find safety. 

I left this book most feeling understanding this is why it’s important to choose reading authors of color who are part of the community and culture they’re writing about rather than reading a popular book.

review:
Perhaps one of the best tech books I've read, very relevant for our current time, and will be recommending to friends interested in learning what AI is and what its significance is. 

The book is different from other what-is-AI books in that it places AI in context of current events, historical realities, and what could potentially happen. Perhaps the most intriguing part of this book is part 3, where Kanaan describes AI's impact on global relations - providing a very convincing argument that the US needs to up it's game in defining a vision for AI as a democratic ideal. 

Part I of the book is not really about AI, but rather a brief history of technology and knowledge, which makes the potential impact of AI seem extraordinarily significant. Instead of simply talking about '600 years ago the Guttenberg press changed the world and so will AI', he sets the stage for how and why data is important for knowledge expansion, and how technologies influence on knowledge expansion shaped civilizations. At first I thought starting off the history of the world with the literal history of the world was a pedantic excuse to show off Kanaan's knowledge, but after finishing the book I have gained a different mental model on how to think about knowledge, data, and civilization growth.

Part II explains knowledge through the lens of data and also provides a very fascinating exploration of the evolvement of technology. Here he explains in exquisitely simple language what AI is -- as someone in the tech world who has from time to time needed to explain things like big data, AI, and other terminologies, I will be stealing some of the ways Kanaan conveyed AI to provide that imagery to others. Kanaan has a brilliant way of explaining AI in a concise and understandable way.

Part III was the most interesting part. I had picked this book up because Kanaan works at the Pentagon. I have been interested in hearing a military perspective of technology, particularly in the wake of China's massive expansion of AI. Kanaan provides a frightening, and yet not hyperbolic, picture of what authoritarian governments are in the process of doing with AI, and how without a counter-weight to their cyber imperial expansions, it can massively shift the global balance. Simultaneously, he exposes what is probably the weakness of democracy, an institution that has only existed for a few hundred years, when it comes to misinformation. 

"An uninformed, misinformed, or disinformed electorate is no real electorate at all - as an unaware of confused voting base compromises the most critical component in the basic philosophy upon which democracy rests" Authoritarian governments have been able to succeed in the AI race because they can control information, and, in light of the previous election of Trump, disinformation is demonstrating massive weaknesses in the American system of government. 

Nevertheless, again, the most convincing Kanaan provides is the need to promote a democratic ideal in the AI world, as a Sputnik moment. As in, we need to think about AI the same way people thought about sending a man on the moon, it was a requirement to defend a democratic institution. After finishing this book, I thought about how it feels like in America most AI development is done in the private sphere from a capitalistic lens - how both large corporations to individuals are looking to make profit off of AI through exploitative and non-exploitative practices. Meaning that Americans are not seeing AI as a Sputnik moment, a place where we need to come together and promote values of what AI should ethically look like. Instead, we're all looking to get on the AI train and mine gold, where only the people who sell the shovels are going to get rich. With this in mind, I fear for America's future, how in the world are we going to compete with authoritarian governments?

review:
If I took away anything from this book it’s the idea that perhaps the field of UX’s foundation was libertarian propaganda. 

Freedom, which is a central concept of this book, is not well defined and feels like a plastic world. 

Perhaps the most disgusting example of freedom is at the very beginning the idea that men need to have games added to urinals so they aim better. The problem with freedom as very loosely and idealistically defined here is that we also have responsibility, the bare minimum is probably not to leave urine around in the bathroom because you somehow were not budged to be conscious that other humans exist and need to use the same facilities. 

Overall, glad I read the book, hated the themes.

title: The Hard Thing About Hard Things: Building a Business When There Are No Easy Answers―Straight Talk on the Challenges of Entrepreneurship
author: Ben Horowitz
review:
There are parts of this book that contradict itself, but I guess the one thing I learned from this books is the job of the ceo is to figure out how to strategically respond with limited information and a lot of risk. He writes that he cares about his employees but I didn’t get that sense entirely, the management techniques as compared to say Julie Zhou’s book, yes meant for beginners tho this is technically a book for beginner ceos, is a lot less emphatic and more about the goal in mind - you can sacrifice anything and everyone to achieve that goal. 

The advice in general is great because the book talks about making all the decisions that are truly hard to make and attempts to be objective about it. I didn’t understand a lot of his generalized statements, such as all engineers like to swear. 

The low rating is mostly for the first few chapters of the book - especially the opening of the book - how does a person start a book talking about inviting 100 of his closest friends and that his black friends called him the Jackie Robinson of BBQ? And he “crossed the color line.” For a book that argues so often about the effectiveness of being direct, authentic and non-ego-centric I found the authors personality to be antithetical to what he was preaching. Also, I don’t understand how anyone can get away with starting off a book with a childhood story about how they didn’t say the n-word and that changed their life... it really bothered me that he, as a white man, wrote out a word we cannot when say out loud. The reason I’m highlighting this is because this sort of tone-deafness carried throughout the book, and it made me dislike the author and wonder if I should take the advice seriously. 

Hoping to read other management books and gain more than from this, but overall hope that more experienced people write specifically on this topic - the hard thing about hard things so we can get multiple perspectives and strategies on this.

review: I'm not sure if I was the right audience for this book. I came in thinking I was to read a secular, historical account of Jesus, but what was received was confusing. The book is divided into three (not clearly defined) parts. The first is a historical description of what was happening around the time of Jesus, the second is a biography of Jesus, and the last is how the idea of Jesus Christ formed after his crucifixion. In every part I felt confused as to where this was going, Aslan went back and forth in history and time to insert ideas to explain why x was happening, but also showing that this predicted a future of y. I think the best audience for this book is someone well versed in Christianity who may be questioning the reliability of the story of Jesus. I learned a lot, but, also have a lot more questions.

title: Rich Dad Poor Dad: What the Rich Teach Their Kids About Money—That the Poor and Middle Class Do Not!
author: Robert T. Kiyosaki
review:
Note: I know next to nothing about money 

This book is a must read, but not to get rich - instead to get a novice understanding of the mindset of the rich. As I was reading this I kept thinking of Voldemort’s famous quote, “there is no good and evil. There is only power and those too weak to seek it.” This book helped me understand why Elizabeth Warren is proposing capital gains taxes, and why income taxes aren’t the most useful! It also helped me realize how GOP pushed a certain tax plan that helped corporations — and left me thinking perhaps the general uninformed public (aka me) are choosing the wrong scapegoat —- huge corporations. When really it’s much more sinister and complicated than that. 

First, to move to personal value of this book - the chapter that describes how to think of your life through assets and liabilities is perhaps the most valuable. I also like the idea of paying yourself first, and want to try this 2020 to see if it creates a shift in my own approach to personal finances.

The most fascinating chapter was on corporations. He advises immediately the best way to keep your money is by opening a corporation. Not a startup that one intends to one day become the next Microsoft. A holding company that can help one evade income taxes, as corporate taxes are much lower. It made me realize, as stupid as I am for not realizing this earlier, why Elon Musk recently claimed he doesn’t have any cash on him. He like many others are hiding their money in places like this. This book was written in the 90s so things have probably changed and I’m curious to learn more.

We even learn that rich make foundations — things that give to charity — to further enrich themselves. 

He even recommends insider trading as long as it’s not illegal. One thing I found extremely unethical is that he uses his company to pay for personal things — like cars, dinners, flights, etc. and labels them as a business expense so he can pay for that before it gets taxed. 

Perhaps the most enlightening thing about this was how the rich approach taxes. The “poor” dad is really a well paid man who believes taxes help with redistribution of wealth and finds it his civic duty. The “rich” dad believes taxes are only ways to take his earned money away, and that most of us are working for the government for four months a year. So, he learned to evade taxes. The best way to do that is avoid high taxes like income taxes, next is to learn tax loopholes that’ll help him evade further taxes.

Rich dad’s reasoning for this — money is power and people with power make the laws. They make laws to benefit themselves and will protect their money. Evading taxes is just what rich people do. Eventually the “Robin Hood” tax mentality — taking money from rich and distributing it to the poor — doesn’t work because the rich are smart enough to avoid paying. In the end the middle class ends up paying the most percentage of taxes. 

This book angered me in many ways, I know it’s a popular book and therefore probably not the genuine philosophy rich people follow, but even if it’s a small breadth of what is happening, it’s horrifying. The bizarre part is that the author thinks he’s a good person since he’s teaching other people these secrets to richness rather than seeing this as part of the problem. 

I do appreciate the insight into empathizing with people who think like this, because I guess it’s not really good vs evil for them, but a completely different way of thinking. It has made me wonder if there is a different way to think about how to approach the Uber wealthy and help them think of more than themselves.

title: Creative Confidence: Unleashing the Creative Potential Within Us All
author: Tom Kelley
review:
I used this book to come up with ideas for a workshop I'm hosting at work; some of the ideas I shared with the team and we're implementing them. So in terms of getting things on the ground running found this book to be useful.

On a personal level, I found this book motivating and encouraging, and also enjoyed the optimistic language to push oneself beyond their comfort zone and embrace who they are as a naturally creative person (the inner child within us all). The ideas on how to boost creative confidence are doable and fun. I feel encourage to pursue my individual pursuits and can see myself recommending this to a friend who has a creative idea but doesn't feel the push or is hesitant about pursuing it. 

At the same time, I found the book frustrating, particularly in its promotion of act first, ask for forgiveness later. Creating problems that didn't exist, and then iterating on fixing those problems is what created a lot of the Silicon Valley mess we see right now. Design thinking is almost far too idealistic, like a fairy godmother showing up dazzling everyone with her magic. It's in a sense mythical, and in some ways I found it morally irresponsible. 

I almost feel like we're being imprisoned by a cult like mentality when there's so little criticism of design thinking. Limiting everything to design sprints and acting as quickly as possible, rather than thinking through as to what the consequences are of causing this disruption is problematic in my mind. Innovators of the past were respected because of the amount of effort they put into to become experts of their field, there is something missing in our society today when we don't respect those who dedicate their lives to be an expert and instead blindly make everyone an equal. I would trust experts to be able to understand the ethical, social, environmental, economic, etc. consequences of introducing a new disruptive idea into the world. I get that design thinking came about to restructure the tired old ways of corporate America, so I hope there is a way we can balance these methods. 

I also read reviews before starting this book that this felt like a 300 page brochure for d.school, and I have to agree with them.

title: A Letter to a Hindu
author: Leo Tolstoy
review:
"It is natural for men to help and to love one another, but not to torture and to kill one another."

My favorite part of this book was perhaps a one sentence statement about how love, the highest virtue and most natural force of human nature, was relegated to a private space and ignored in the public. Written before the World Wars, this letter speaks passionately about nonviolent resistance, particularly in the case of India where a corporation of feeble, weak men was able to capture and subordinate a nation of 200 million. Towards the end, he also briefly acknowledges the plight in North America for black Americans. 

I love reading about love and how important and natural it is for each of us to love. I enjoyed reading about our structures of reality and how 'science' has replaced 'religion' as a means to control people's minds and desensitize them to senseless violence. I particularly enjoyed how he writes how all religions have a singular truth which is to love. And his plea for nonviolent resistance was beautiful, however unrealistic.

It is a very short read, and therefore extremely high-level writing, not something that one can take apart and apply directly to their lives, but perhaps writing to challenge the structure of reality we currently accept without thinking too hard about it. Are there ways to respond with love, a natural state, a fitra, over violence in our life currently - whether it be in our private or public life? I'm not sure if any of my review makes sense, and if I'll get what I was trying to convey when I read this months from now, but I'm ok with that. I like that my response to this was nebulous. 

I don't believe resistance against oppression can be completed entirely nonviolently. Particularly in the case of black Americans in North America, where lynching was made a federal crime in 2018, and systemic racism still exists.

title: The Power
author: Naomi Alderman
review:
The book has a fascinating premise - what would the world look like if women suddenly developed the power to electrify/hurt people with just their hands? Women would be able to fight back. Fight back against human trafficking, oppressive governments (like Saudi), and turn the playing cards.

The first half of the book where women realize this power and start to use it is fascinating, but from then on it goes a bit too far. I started first thinking of The Crucible, since the power is given mostly to teenaged girls who, having less experience with life, use it for their own selfish power-hungry means. The book then becomes more violent as women seem to do nothing more than reverse the power order, becoming what men are at this moment. Establishing anti-men laws and making it more difficult for men to exist.

In a way, it's an interesting way to portray how men in our current world have established power over women. I'm not entirely sure if that was what the book was supposed to be a metaphor of -- since it is quite disturbing to read about women pillaging and raping men at refugee camps.

If I'm wrong about that, I don't really believe if women were given this power we'd end up in some sort of cultish world within ten years. The book does nothing to defend femininity, assumes it's a response to masculinity because masculinity defines our current world order. But, women are existing in a world established over thousands of years, where we are loving and caring. The idea that we would all accept violence as a new world order seems absurd, almost ridiculous.... But then again, it only took a few years for half of America to believe a racist theory brown people are invading our borders down south and only a wall could stop them. 

I think I'd like this book more if it wasn't just about power-hungry women, but also those who still want to spread love and kindness and more femininity in the world.

title: Prediction Machines: The Simple Economics of Artificial Intelligence
author: Ajay Agrawal
review:
This book stressed me out. 

For someone who is unsure what AI is and what its impact will be this book provides great, simple non-technical explanation of AI from an economic perspective. For technical people, it provides a way to structure your thoughts on how to approach and see the value of various AI tools, as well as presents a way to explain AI to non-technical people. In essence, it has transformed my way of seeing machine learning/AI into something very easy to explain within a structured framework, which is probably the most valuable asset of this book. And a very important asset. 

This book won't last very long in terms of the value of its advice, as the ideas expressed in this book will either rapidly start happening soon, so if someone wants to understand AI and what's coming this is a now or never book to read. 

The neutral, and sometimes almost awed tone, of the book made me queasy. It's probably paranoia, but I'm not sure if I want to wash myself of the paranoia.

I found myself writing notes on the margins throughout the book questioning the ethics and what will come of society afterwards. I've been a bit nervous about the future with AI, and after reading this I was left with a dystopic nightmare in my mind of almost half the population out of jobs through elimination of most if not all blue-color jobs as well as many white-collar jobs, the stress one would feel to have to constantly feel like they need to perpetually be the best before AI decides they need to be eliminated from the job, and countries with low human rights records or conversations about the ethics of AI being at the forefront of a new world order. The authors answer all those stressful conversations in a short chapter - I think there was one sentence dedicated to how they believe it's possible for there to be an AI Recession. 

Along with that, there was very little focus on who is developing the AI and the biases that are inputted into it - there were a few pages dedicated to racism and gender biases, but not enough to make me feel confident that tech world will be able to resolve it.

They mention the famous Putin quote about whoever advances AI will rule the world, what happens when that's a company (rather than a country) not subject to laws made and formed over time by people? 

Anyway, lots of questions, lots of stress I've been left with.

title: The Seasons of the Soul
author: Hermann Hesse
review: I am not an avid reader of poetry, and when I initially started reading this I thought this was a good 101 book since the metaphors and allusions are fairly easy to grasp. But, this book ended up being much more, the words feel like you're outside on a day where the sun is beaming lightly on you and a gentle breeze flows by you. It's cathartic, filled with common sense wisdom we tend to forget. Spiritually a reminder of why we're here, and a contemplative look on how to approach everything. He writes in a very relatable way, sometimes I felt like it was written just for me. A good book for learning how to fit in spiritually in a modern world.

title: One Thousand and One Nights
author: Hanan Al-Shaykh
review:
There is something weirdly innocent about this book. Although it is filled with sexuality, the ideals and morals it advocates are tinged with innocence that can only be told through dazzling oral tales. It's easy to see how these are tales that were passed orally, perhaps over a campfire or other communal gathering meant for fun, bawdy tales with very obvious life lessons in between. 

Women in the book are mischievous, but also have a sense of unrealistic, idealistic loyalty, love, and patience that perhaps come from an scintillating understanding of Islam. The way some women are treated made me tear up, for it reminded me of that famous Khaled Hosseini quote “A man's heart is a wretched, wretched thing. It isn't like a mother's womb. It won't bleed. It won't stretch to make room for you.” Some of the demands men make on women is horrific, and made me wonder if perhaps these tales also demonstrate how patriarchy and oppression was passed through a lens of Islam and sexist culture. 

Overall, think I read this at the right time for myself, as I'm at a place wondering if Muslim men are more than the characters in this book - where they are loyal, courageous and daring when it comes to themselves and other men, but are quite different towards the women in their lives.

title: Songs of Blood and Sword: A Daughter's Memoir
author: Fatima Bhutto
review: No one can deny that Fatima Bhutto is a good writer. The book is enjoyable to read, but provides an incredibly one-sided approach to Pakistani politics. If she focused more on the 'memoir' part rather than politics I probably would have given this a higher rating. The entire time I read the book I felt she was trying to convert me to her beliefs on Pakistani politics with very biased information. She doesn't approach the history/politics of Pakistan in an objective manner due to the fact that she is unable to let go of her family name when discussing the topic. She quickly dismisses the negatives of the family members she loves, and tries to convince us that those who disagree with those family members are evil/corrupt/etc. I think I can understand that she would hero-worship her father and grandfather, especially since they both did not die from natural deaths, but a consequence of that is she has an inability to approach these figures in a critical manner. In the beginning of the book she mentions that her thesis adviser warns her that a dissertation she was writing on her grandfather was too hagiographic, and I do not think that adviser would even consider this book as a work of scholarship. As such, when I read this I had to constantly remind myself that the subtitle is "A Daughter's Memoir."
